name: Profit Margin

claims.claim_text: The figure the industry converges on is roughly 2.4 times bill-of-materials cost, and that is the absolute minimum for the exercise to be worth doing rather than a target.
claims.quote_verbatim: minimum is like 2.4 times your bomb cost everyone talks about
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: A transparent pricing model of 2.6 times the bill of materials is built from two stacked 40 percent margins — one for the wholesaler and one for the retailer — with nothing charged for the intellectual property. Priced that way, a competitor can undercut you by roughly one of those margins and no further while still making money.
claims.quote_verbatim: 2.6 times the bill of materials. And that number is based on two 40% margins
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: The bootstrapping arithmetic sets the floor: ten percent profit on a batch of ten boards funds exactly one more board. Growing without outside money requires better than doubling your money, which is the real reason the multiplier is two and a half rather than something more modest.
claims.quote_verbatim: you make 10 boards. For example. And you make 10 percent profit. Well. You've only got enough profit to buy one more board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Cash Is King

claims.claim_text: A kit business needs three to four times parts cost. Twenty percent profit describes a good conventional business, and a kit sold at parts cost plus twenty or fifty percent returns so little that the time is better spent elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: got to sell it for three or four times what the parts cost is
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Adafruit, Chip heist, Hackerspaces - The Kit Conniption

claims.claim_text: Make the first run small — twenty-five units — and set the price so that run alone recovers the one-off costs, the board tooling included. If the margin cannot repay the setup within the first small batch, the pricing is wrong before volume enters the picture.
claims.quote_verbatim: do your first run of kits small and base your profit margin based on
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Adafruit, Chip heist, Hackerspaces - The Kit Conniption

claims.claim_text: Driving down bill-of-materials cost deserves the overwhelming share of the effort, because a low parts cost is what gives you somewhere to retreat to when a competitor appears or the market shifts — margin held in reserve is optionality, not greed.
claims.quote_verbatim: go spend 90% of your time trying to get the cost as low as physically possible
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Adafruit, Chip heist, Hackerspaces - The Kit Conniption

claims.claim_text: Taking the parts cost and adding twenty percent is the standard beginner's error in hardware pricing, because it accounts for none of the costs between the parts arriving and the customer receiving the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: you look at your bomb cost and then I'll add 20% or something for your margin and that just doesn't work
claims.speaker: Jonathan Oxer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: Every party in the chain takes a margin and the price compounds as it passes along, with the last party before the customer usually taking the largest share — which is why a price that looks generous at the factory gate looks thin at retail.
claims.quote_verbatim: the last person in the food chain makes the highest margin
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: Handing a product to a distributor typically returns ten to fifteen percent where selling it yourself might return most of the margin. The gap buys fulfilment, marketing reach and the absence of individual order handling, and the decision turns on whether you want that work rather than on the percentage.
claims.quote_verbatim: who might give you, you know, 15%, 10% of the thing instead of making 80% profit
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: Accepting less income per unit in exchange for someone else handling fulfilment is a legitimate and deliberate trade rather than a failure to negotiate, and it is the right one for anyone whose time is better spent designing the next product.
claims.quote_verbatim: he's traded off hassle
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Spacing Out On Space - Dave's Dongle Designing

claims.claim_text: A marketplace typically takes around ten percent where a self-hosted store costs a fixed monthly fee, so the percentage model only makes sense above a volume where the flat cost is smaller — and on low-margin goods a percentage fee can consume most of what is left.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's about 10%. Something like that. Whereas your e-commerce store is nothing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Science, Not Silence

claims.claim_text: Payment processing takes a few percent of the transaction regardless of what the product earns, so any business running at a low single-digit margin has already given its entire profit to the card network.
claims.quote_verbatim: sell ice cream cones with a 3% margin. And then Visa takes 3
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: Pure distribution is structurally a race to the bottom: whatever margin you accept, someone will accept half of it, and customers will move. Distributors that survive do so on the other things they provide rather than on the resale itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: another guy comes along, he sells it. He's happy with a 5% margin. You're screwed
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Art Of Staying Interested In Electronics - Exponible Electronics Ennui

claims.claim_text: Selling direct keeps both the margin the channel would take and the customer relationship, and the relationship is arguably worth more: knowing who buys what, in what quantity, is exactly the information a manufacturer needs to decide what to build next.
claims.quote_verbatim: they buy them direct, and we have terms
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: Consolidation among distributors is a margin story: as the percentage available on each transaction falls, scale becomes the only way to keep the absolute number up, and acquisition is the fastest route to scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: reason that Avnet grows by an arrow and these big ones grow by acquisitions because their margins are getting squeezed
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mergers and Acquiescence

claims.claim_text: Twenty percent annual profit marks a genuinely good business in an ordinary industry. On twenty million of turnover that is two million, before tax and before it is split among the owners — which is the scale check to apply before treating a revenue figure as impressive.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're making 20% profit per year, you are a really good business
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Open Source RC & Modelsource - Facinorous Financial Foulness

claims.claim_text: Revenue reveals almost nothing on its own: 1.4 billion in annual revenue against 45 million in profit is about three percent, the same order as a grocery store, and a far smaller business at a better margin can be worth more to its owner.
claims.quote_verbatim: had $1.4 billion in annual revenue and their profit was $45 million
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Consolidate All The Things - Zonked Zelotic Zaitech

claims.claim_text: A hardware business turning over a million dollars a year can pay its owner less than an employed engineer earns, because the margin available in its segment is what determines take-home pay rather than the size of the revenue line.
claims.quote_verbatim: the margins are very slim because of the area that they operate in
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Firmware, Netburner and Semiconductors - Chris's Capitalism Colloquy

claims.claim_text: Two quite different businesses reach the same revenue: one selling large volumes of thirty-dollar products, which requires enormous shipping throughput and the staff to handle it, and one selling a few high-value products with a handful of people. The margin structure, not the revenue, sets the headcount.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've got to sell a lot of stuff. They've got to ship a lot, a lot of volume
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Cost Of Doing Business

claims.claim_text: A ten million dollar business run at twenty percent throws off two million a year and can be built without venture money at all — a contrarian position holding that you should set out to build a good company rather than an exit, on the argument that a good company gets found at the right time anyway.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you can create a $10 million business, which is about the size of a dry cleaning franchise, and you can manage it so it's throwing off 20% profit
claims.speaker: Steve Liebson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Steve Leibson - Impavid Ideopraxist Insider

claims.claim_text: Partnering deeply with one manufacturer bought a small company near-large-volume pricing, and margins were then raised gradually rather than opportunistically. The payoff was predictability: knowing costs from build to build determined how many people could be employed and how many new designs could be started.
claims.quote_verbatim: we gently nudged up our margins, but we never went to an extreme
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: In a high-volume consumer product, every component that could be removed already has been, because at volume each part removed is margin straight to the bottom line — which is why such a board looks sparse next to an equivalent industrial one.
claims.quote_verbatim: you will never find a component in a cell phone or any kind of commercial product that does not need to be in there
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Cores, Digikey, Electronic Design - The Commercial Competitor Commencement

claims.claim_text: A demand for more margin is a routine trigger for redesigning a working product, with a target expressed in cents per unit rather than in features — which is a different engineering problem from the one that produced the original design.
claims.quote_verbatim: need to make more profit margin or something like that. So we need to slash two cents off the price
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: OSHW, Makerbot & Memristo - Maundering Memristor Mathematicaster

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor integration is margin-driven from the vendor's side: absorbing a function that used to be a separate chip lets them sell one part that costs the customer less in total solution cost while capturing more of the value themselves.
claims.quote_verbatim: every chip especially is going to have higher and higher levels of integration because that's how all these companies see their margins improving
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Documentation Is A Waste Of Time

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor pricing carries margin deliberately, because it funds the fab, the applications engineers and the sales organisation — which is why vendors resist anything that erodes it and why free support is not actually free.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have priced in the margin or, you know, supposed to be high just because they have a lot of support
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Automation Amish

claims.claim_text: Instrument vendors capable of collapsing the price of a high-end capability decline to, because doing so destroys the margin pool for the whole market including themselves. The restraint is not collusion so much as everyone independently declining to undercut their own product line.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can offer you know a one gigahertz scope for a hundred bucks you're not going to do it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kismetic Keithley Katowse

claims.claim_text: Development boards carry deliberately lower margin than production hardware, and are frequently booked as marketing rather than as product — which is why their pricing tells you nothing about the economics of the parts they showcase.
claims.quote_verbatim: you do give your dev boards a lower profit margin than your production boards
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: Stick 'Em On Whales

claims.claim_text: Where a product is manufactured is evidence about its margin: assembly in a high-wage country implies the price supports it, which usually means a strong brand and a premium the market accepts.
claims.quote_verbatim: audio stuff has a significant margin. If it's being made in Sydney, it has a significant margin
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Secret Buzzer Handshake

claims.claim_text: The common crowdfunding failure is not missing the target but hitting it: the campaign funds, and then the creator discovers the pricing left no margin to survive manufacture. Basing prices on local assembly costs and distributor part pricing is the conservative way to avoid it.
claims.quote_verbatim: not actually going to make anything out of this because I didn't leave enough margin
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Before collecting money, four things have to be settled: the cash flow, the margins, who is manufacturing, and reward tiers priced from real quotes rather than estimates. Doing this afterwards is what turns a funded campaign into an obligation you cannot meet.
claims.quote_verbatim: understanding what your cash flow is, understanding what your margins are, who your manufacturer is, and actually basing those rewards off of real quotes
claims.speaker: Zach Dunham
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: Yield is a pricing input, not a manufacturing detail: pricing at twenty percent margin and then achieving eighty percent yield means every fifth unit's cost has to come out of that twenty percent, which it cannot.
claims.quote_verbatim: maybe 20% margin at the offset was a bad idea after I had 80% yield
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Kerry Scharfglass

claims.claim_text: Costing a bill of materials in one currency and selling in another puts the margin at the mercy of the exchange rate — a twelve percent move in parts cost against a planned margin can consume most of it without anything changing in the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: my parts cost 12 percent more than what I anticipated on my bomb because my bomb was in US dollars
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A 2013 Recap - Year-end Yarn Yakking

claims.claim_text: Purchase quantity feeds straight through to margin: buying in small lots raises the per-part cost and shrinks what is left, while buying volume improves it and ties up cash in inventory you now have to hold and track. There is no position that optimises both.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I'm now buying them in smaller quantities, that is a higher cost per part, and that means my margin goes down
claims.speaker: Jan Rychter
claims.episode_title: Component Management with Jan Rychter

claims.claim_text: On precision parts the gap between single-piece and volume pricing is severe enough to decide the product — four dollars against twelve for one resistor, with the difference coming directly out of margin at low volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're paying four bucks a resistor instead of maybe the single piece price for one would be like 12 bucks
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: PLEASE be a die shrink

claims.claim_text: Designers routinely underprice their work out of discomfort with charging for it, treating the need to make money as something to apologise for. It is a learned skill rather than a character trait, and the usual teacher is running out of money.
claims.quote_verbatim: lot of designers. Like. . . Are ashamed. About the fact that they. . . That they need money
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: New Year Education

claims.claim_text: Regular price increases are normal in most industries and resisted in maker and hobbyist markets, where sellers would rather absorb the cost than appear to be gouging. The result harms buyers too, because a seller with no margin does not stay in business — and electronics is unusual in that the same part genuinely does get cheaper each year, which trains exactly the wrong expectation.
claims.quote_verbatim: people should probably be raising their prices, but I think there's also resistance to that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pavlovian Cheapskates

claims.claim_text: Manufacturing location follows the margin structure rather than preference: consumer margins are thin enough to require offshore volume pricing, while industrial products rarely have the volume to justify it and are better served locally.
claims.quote_verbatim: going to get you the margins that you need for consumer
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Secret Squirrel

claims.claim_text: In fast-moving consumer categories the window to earn back a design is on the order of four months, after which price competition removes the margin — which changes what level of engineering investment the product can carry.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have like four months to make all of their money
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Idiorhythmic IPC Inconcinnity

claims.claim_text: Consumer categories differ enormously in the margin they allow, and toys sit near the bottom — tight enough that the engineering decisions available differ in kind from those in a wearable or an industrial product.
claims.quote_verbatim: did toys for LeapFrog and that was even more consumery than Fitbit was because their profit margin was tiny
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pedantic or Andrantic

claims.claim_text: Adding connectivity to a mature commodity product is usually a margin response rather than a user requirement: once copies erode the price of a well-made kettle, a feature nobody asked for is the cheapest available differentiator.
claims.quote_verbatim: do you start to differentiate? Well, you differentiate by saying, now with Bluetooth
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Photon Rich, Cash Poor

claims.claim_text: A product retailing at two hundred and fifty dollars that returns sixty to its maker is the argument for becoming a services business rather than a hardware one, because that share will not sustain the organisation that built it.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're selling it for 250 bucks, but you know, only 60 of that is going towards the company
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mapping Out Nerdery

claims.claim_text: Selling into an industry that itself runs on thin margins constrains the product hard: it has to work every time, cost little and be simple enough to need no attention, because the buyer has no headroom to absorb either the price or the failure.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're trying to sell a piece of technology to a farmer and they're like on super razor thin margins
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Return of the Trade Show Jedi

claims.claim_text: Valuation claims can be checked with one multiplication: at sixty percent margin on a two hundred dollar product, justifying a 3.2 billion dollar price means selling 250 million units over the product's life — a number that immediately fails a sanity check for a niche device.
claims.quote_verbatim: a 60% margin on a $200 product, right? Right. That requires 250 million products
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Manufacturing By Wire And Skipping Testing - Calefacient Cuculine Cash

claims.claim_text: The same check applied elsewhere: around two million boards a year with roughly eighty percent of income from hardware does not produce the profit that would support a valuation in the hundreds of millions, whatever the brand is worth.
claims.quote_verbatim: sell about 2 million boards a year
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Welding with an HDMI Cable

claims.claim_text: When an acquisition price cannot be justified by units sold or by margin, and the technology is largely open anyway, what is being bought is the brand and the community around it — and that is a legitimate purchase, just not the one the financial framing suggests.
claims.quote_verbatim: didn't buy them for the financials
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Google Glass, Lean Startup and VotC - Initializing Instructed Interviews

claims.claim_text: A company sitting on cash converts it into margin by pre-buying components at enormous volume — whole production runs at a time — which is also the argument for buying a supplier outright: owning it removes someone else's margin from your own cost base.
claims.quote_verbatim: they use that cash that they've built up to buy, you know, 10 or 100 million processors
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Two and a Half Orders of Magnitude

claims.claim_text: Hardware and software businesses differ in cash flow more than in margin: hardware ties money up in parts before anything can be sold, while a software business commits almost nothing to inventory — which is why the two need such different amounts of working capital for the same revenue.
claims.quote_verbatim: the margins are tighter because you have to buy all the parts, you have to have the cash flow freed up
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Cash Is King

claims.claim_text: Hardware cost savings are real and nearly impossible to claim credit for: a salesperson points at a million dollars of new business, while an engineer who took ten cents off one board of a twenty-product line has improved margin invisibly.
claims.quote_verbatim: reused a MOSFET and I was able to save us 10 cents per board
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Electrical Archeology

attribution_notes: attribution_reliable was not trusted. ep105 (Chris Anderson), ep99 (Steve Leibson), ep302 (Clint Cole), ep350 (Zach Dunham), ep542 (Jan Rychter) and ep123 (Jonathan Oxer) label host questions with the guest's name; only material unambiguously the guest's own was used.
ep113 records the Scott Miller interview with the guest under a machine speaker label; the claim kept is Dave Jones's own pricing advice, which is unambiguous in context.
ep368 and ep410 attribute the same passage alternately to both hosts; the manufacturing-location inference is kept and attributed to Dave Jones by content.

Speculation about specific company valuations, acquisition gossip and currency politics was excluded except where a stated arithmetic method is transferable — the unit-count and margin sanity checks were kept for the method, not the verdict.
